title: Review: Sources of genetic variation in meiosis and fertilisation; Meiosis; Cell specialisation, tissues, organs; Stem cells
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CD03#t4 term and clue written for the game; CD04#t1 term and clue written for the game; CD03#t1 term and clue written for the game; CD04#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD03#N.6, CD04#N.6, CE07a#N.10b, CE08a#N.2, CD03#N.10a, CD04#N.4, CE07a#N.11, CE08a#N.8, CD03#N.3, CD04#N.13, CE07a#N.3a, CD03#N.8. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Homologous chromosomes
items.clue: A matching maternal and paternal pair with the same genes at the same loci

items.label: Crossing over
items.clue: Exchange of equivalent sections between non-sister chromatids in prophase I

items.label: Diploid
items.clue: Having two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent; 46 in a human body cell

items.label: Independent assortment
items.clue: Random orientation of each homologous pair at metaphase I, whatever the other pairs do

questions.stem: Which statement correctly outlines the two rounds of segregation in meiosis?

options.text: In meiosis I the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated, and in meiosis II the homologous chromosomes of each pair are separated.
In meiosis I the two chromosomes of each homologous pair separate; in meiosis II the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate.
In meiosis I the homologous chromosomes are separated; the DNA is then replicated so that meiosis II can separate the new chromatids.
In meiosis I each chromosome is split into its maternal chromatid and its paternal chromatid, and meiosis II shares these between nuclei.

questions.explanation: Meiosis I is the reduction division: the two chromosomes of each bivalent go to opposite poles. Meiosis II separates the two chromatids of each of those chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which statement describes crossing over during meiosis?

options.text: The two sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange their segments in prophase I.
At a chiasma, all four chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments in prophase I.
Non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments in prophase I.
Homologous pairs swap the sides of the plate they face at metaphase I.

questions.explanation: While homologues are paired in prophase I, non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding segments at chiasmata, making new combinations of alleles.

questions.stem: The wall of the stomach contains epithelium, smooth muscle and connective tissue. Together they digest and churn food. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Epithelium, muscle and connective tissue are each organs, as each has a function.
The stomach is an organ system, as it contains several different tissues.
The stomach is an organ: several tissues working together for an overall function.
Epithelium is not a tissue if it contains goblet cells as well as other cells.

questions.explanation: Epithelium, muscle and connective tissue each do one job; together they perform digestion, the stomach's overall function.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties defines a stem cell?

options.text: Capacity to divide endlessly and ability to differentiate along different pathways.
Ability to divide whenever a tissue is damaged and to produce more cells of its own type.
Ability to switch from one specialised type to another whenever a tissue requires this.
Continuous division at all times, giving new cells whether or not they are needed.

questions.explanation: A stem cell can divide endlessly, and it can differentiate along different pathways to give specialised cell types. Both are required.

questions.stem: A student counts chromosomes in dividing cells of a hypothetical plant species with 2n = 40. Which prediction is correct for the number of chromosomes in each daughter cell at the end of mitosis in a root-tip cell and at the end of meiosis II in an anther cell?

options.text: Root tip: 20; anther: 40
Root tip: 40; anther: 40
Root tip: 40; anther: 20
Root tip: 20; anther: 10

questions.explanation: Mitosis keeps the parent's number (40). Meiosis halves it in meiosis I and keeps it in meiosis II: 20.

questions.stem: Garden peas have a diploid number of 14. Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes can random orientation of bivalents produce in the gametes?

options.text: 7 different combinations
14 different combinations
16 384 different combinations
128 different combinations

questions.explanation: 2n = 14 means 7 bivalents. Each can face either way, independently: 2⁷ = 128.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical species of plant, leaf cells make large amounts of a protein that binds chlorophyll, but the root cells of the same plant make none of it. Which statement best explains this difference?

options.text: In root cells, the base sequence of the gene has been changed, and the gene no longer codes for the protein.
Both cell types carry the gene for the protein, but it is expressed in leaf cells and not in root cells.
Root cells have lost the gene for the protein from their DNA because they did not use it.
Root cells do not need the protein, so they choose not to make it, unlike the cells of leaves.

questions.stem: A cell is taken from adult bone marrow and grown in a dish. It divides many times. Some daughter cells stay like the parent; others become erythrocytes, neutrophils and other blood cells, but never nerve or muscle cells. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It cannot be a stem cell, because a stem cell can form every type of body cell.
It is a specialised blood cell that divides whenever more blood is needed.
It is a stem cell, though it can form only a limited range of cell types.
It has lost the genes for nerve and muscle proteins, so it can make only blood cells.

questions.explanation: It divides repeatedly, keeps a population like itself, and differentiates. But only into blood cells, not every body cell.

questions.stem: A diploid nucleus of an organism with 2n = 14 undergoes meiosis. What is produced?

options.text: Four diploid nuclei, each containing 14 chromosomes
Four haploid nuclei, each with half of the organism's genes
Two haploid nuclei, each containing 7 chromosomes
Four haploid nuclei, each containing 7 chromosomes

questions.explanation: Two divisions give four haploid nuclei from one diploid nucleus. 2n = 14, so each has n = 7: one of each homologous pair.

questions.stem: A mutation in a hypothetical species of animal prevents crossing over during meiosis, but meiosis is otherwise normal. Compared with the gametes of a normal individual, which prediction about the gametes of an individual with this mutation is correct?

options.text: Every gamete would be genetically identical, since crossing over is the only source of genetic variation.
They would vary less but still differ, because homologous pairs still orient randomly at metaphase I.
They would vary just as much as before, since crossing over just swaps sister chromatid segments.
Each gamete would carry either the full maternal or the full paternal set of chromosomes.

questions.stem: In a human, a neuron and a liver cell are both descended by mitosis from the same zygote. What is the difference between them once they have differentiated?

options.text: They express different subsets of the same complete set of genes.
They have kept different sets of genes and discarded the rest.
They were set on different paths inside from fertilisation.
They differ only until the body needs to swap them over.

questions.explanation: All cells produced by mitosis from the zygote inherit the full genome. The neuron switches on the genes for its proteins and the liver cell a different set, while both keep every gene.

questions.stem: A hypothetical animal species has a diploid number of 2n = 20. How many chromosomes and how many chromatids are in one of its cells at metaphase II?

options.text: Chromosomes: 10; chromatids: 20
Chromosomes: 20; chromatids: 20
Chromosomes: 20; chromatids: 40
Chromosomes: 10; chromatids: 10

questions.explanation: Meiosis I separated homologues, so a cell at metaphase II has n = 10 chromosomes. Each still has two chromatids: 10 × 2 = 20.
